blocks.text: Witness statement of [NURSE C] (read)

May it please your Lordship, members of the jury, may we begin, please, by reading a statement and looking whilst we do so at some underlying original material referred to by [Nurse C] in a statement she made on 6 February 2019. That is at page 31, top left corner, of the reading bundle provided to the court a day or two ago.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [Nurse C] states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been asked about my involvement with and recollections of a baby called [Baby I] who died at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 23 October 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Prior to providing this statement, I have had the opportunity to review [Baby I]'s notes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The first date I have been asked about was 23 August 2015. I know from records I was [Baby I]'s designated nurse during the day shift on that date, but to be honest, it's not a shift I
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: recall at all. I would have started at 07.30 and taken over care for [Baby I] some time between 07.45 and 08.00 hours."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She then refers to her nursing notes and with Mr Murphy's assistance, it's page J13807, the bottom -- yes, thank you, Mr Murphy, you're ahead of me.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So the upper paragraph of the notes on screen at present, members of the jury. This will be in your additional file, but it's not on the sequence itself.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And everything I refer to in the next hour or so is in the additional file on the iPads.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So you've got the reference there if you want it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Has anyone else got a problem? Just a white screen, is it?
Mr Murphy, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)

For those who have screens that have got material displayed on them, if you go into the additional -- you should find it in the additional documents on the top right-hand side, J13807. There are very few documents in that little section if you want to follow it there or just -- it's on the main screen as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Do you all have active iPads?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)
Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So I was reading [Nurse C]'s statement and she was just about to refer to her notes in relation to her care for [Baby I] on the morning of 23 August 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She says -- and you can see it in front of you:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From my notes written at 09.37 [we'll come to that discrepancy in a moment] I can see she had some blood in her nappy and I asked someone to review her and we were keeping an eye on that, but I don't remember the shift."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So if we look at the screen we'll see the upper paragraph records that [Baby I] was settled in an incubator, she continued
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: on CPAP, no signs of respiratory distress. There was good capillary -- I'm not sure what CBG is, I'll come back to that. She was warm and well perfused, she was tolerating two-hourly feeds of expressed breast milk via the nasogastric tube, abdomen was distended, although that was reported as normal for this baby. Soft, ie the abdomen, veins apparent all over the trunk, her bowels were opening, she was passing urine well, her skin was intact, and mum called at the start of the shift and will be in for the next cares.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Then this line which was added later:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Mum changed nappy at 12.30 and noted small amount of fresh blood in stool, also mucousy. Consultant informed as on ward. [Baby I] otherwise well with only slightly lower temperature."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So pausing there, [Nurse C] noted, as she stated in her statement that I have just read, that she asked someone to review [Baby I]. The nursing note tells us that was a consultant. If Mr Murphy would be good enough to put up another page, which is also in the additional notes, that is to say page 13758, we'll see the corresponding note from [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Consultant review from [Dr B] at 11.15 am on 23 August, which is said to be day 16. It sets out [Baby I]'s age at birth and her adjusted gestational age:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Problems: premature, respiratory distress syndrome, hence CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And they were establishing feeds.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So there, under the familiar symbols that we now have seen many times, her ventilation, the regime set out, the feeding regime set out, the medication.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we continue down the page, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: On examination the baby was settled, she handled well, the chest was clear, the abdomen was soft, the bowel sounds were positive. The plan was to wean her off CPAP as tolerated. There was a cranial ultrasound that had been received and showed that the ventricles were slightly dilated "in good views", which I take to be a reference to where there was a good image of the ventricles available from the ultrasound:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "No blood clot. Guarded chat to parents when we speak to them."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is under the topic of the results of the ultrasound test.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go down to the next page, PTO. Still talking about the ultrasound:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In some view ventricles look big [perhaps]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The doctor thought mostly the views were -- the choroid plexus, that's part of the brain, was there in the view, and there was significant ventriculomegaly, increased size of ventricles and the blood clot:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Advised to repeat the ultrasound next week and monitor the head circumference [I think that is] twice weekly and please do that when she was not on CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go down to the next part of [Dr B]'s examination. So 12.40, [Dr B] spoke to [Baby I]'s mum and explained the ultrasound finding and the fact that it would be repeated next week -- and here is the point recorded in the nursing notes that directed us here in the first place -- and that [Baby I] had had a small amount of blood and mucus in her nappy, a yellow seedy stool.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Otherwise the temperature was between 36.5 and 36.6.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She was otherwise well and their plan of action was set out:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "CRP and blood count tests. A low threshold for screening."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the plan for the future. The abdominal X-ray should be performed to consider whether NEC was present and samples from the stool should be sent away for examination, and all of this was explained to [Baby I]'s mum.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So if we go back, please, Mr Murphy, to [Nurse C]'s note, thank you very much. We can see how she recorded that event:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Mum changed nappy at 12.30 and noted small amount of fresh blood in stool, also mucousy. The consultant, [we now know that's [Dr B]] was informed. [Baby I] otherwise well with only a slightly low temperature. Stool was sent for reducing substances, FBC and CPR sent. CRP [at that point] 4. WCC raised, but lower than previous result. SPR [probably the senior paediatric registrar] was made aware. Observe for now. Abdo remains distended, soft, veiny, unchanged from previously. Further stool at 16.30 hours free from obvious blood and mucous, yellow and slightly orange in colour. Passing urine well. Warm and well perfused. Observations stable."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we just go to the other side of this page and the upper part of the same page, 13807, we see [Nurse C]'s note, said to be a continuation, timed at 09.35:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] had a settled day. She was off CPAP for 2.75 hours. Then clustered desats so returned on to CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the oxygen levels and the readings: She was warm and well perfused now, following two times low than normal temperatures earlier. She was tolerating feeds.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: A couple of possets this afternoon. Bowels open, passing urine. Bowels opened earlier as new have seen had fresh blood in it and mucus. That was reviewed by [Dr B]. Blood and stool samples were sent for testing. The same data was set out that we've seen earlier:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Abdo was distended and veiny but soft and unchanged from the morning. The plan was to observe her for now with a low threshold for intervention [as we saw on the notes], if required. The ultrasound results were discussed with mum by [Dr B]. Her skin was intact and the DuoDERM was removed from her face and [I guess that should be 'trunk']. Intact skin underneath. Mum was there for most of the day, attending to [Baby I]'s cares, and her father visited in the evening and he was also updated."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's the nursing note that [Nurse C] used to remind herself of the detail before making the statement that I'm reading to you because she couldn't actually remember the shift. But she tells us that she noted that [Baby I] was settled and on CPAP but was having, periodically, 2 to 3 off it, off the CPAP:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We were putting it back on when she had clustered desaturations. That's not unusual. My notes say she didn't have any increasing oxygen requirements and was warm and well perfused throughout. They are things I would worry about in a baby that had a large abdomen like [Baby I] had. She had good capillary blood gas..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That would be the CBG, the initials I couldn't remember a few minutes ago:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "... which measures the pH and the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood and indicates how well the CPAP is working. I noted that she was tolerating two-hourly feeds of expressed breast milk via her nasogastric tube and her abdomen was distended, which was reported as normal for her. Her abdomen was soft and veins were apparent all over her trunk.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Some babies will have a distended abdomen, which can be due to the CPAP, and this is called CPAP belly, but you wouldn't expect to see the veins. If a baby has a distended tummy then you check to see if it's soft, is it painful to be touched, is the baby
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: pooing, do they have bowel sounds, and do they have these veins? The veins can be a sign of a problem.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My next note is timed at 17.19 hours."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I think that is also on the same page. It is.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the one we looked at in the bottom corner where she reported that her mum had changed her nappy. So we have already looked at this:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I noted that mum changed [Baby I]'s nappy at 12.30 and found a small amount of fresh blood in her stool. It was mucousy and I informed the consultant, [Dr B], who was on the ward. I have read her note so I know it was her. She wrote that she looked at it and ordered an abdominal X-ray and that [Baby I] would be a low threshold for a screen. I didn't see [Dr B] examining [Baby I] and I can't remember whether she did or not."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Going back to [Nurse C]'s notes as repeated in her statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I recorded that she had a low (inaudible: coughing) normal temperature of 36.6. Her stool was sent for reducing substances, for an FBC [full blood count] and CRP, which I recorded in error as CPR. CRP is the infection protein that we monitor. The CRP came back with a score of 4 and we were happy with anything less than 10. Her white cell count was raised but lower than previous results and the paediatric registrar was made aware. The plan was to observe for now. Her abdomen remained distended, soft and veiny and unchanged from previously. She had a further stool that was yellow and slightly orange in colour at 16.30 hours and that was free from obvious blood and mucus. She was passing urine well and was warm and well perfused and I observed she was stable. My opinion of [Baby I] at that point was that I had no immediate concerns. We were going to watch her abdomen and watch her bloods.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At 18.27 hours I wrote my evaluation, which is a summary of the day. I recorded that she had been off CPAP for 2.7 hours and she had had a settled day. She then had clustered desats, so went back on to CPAP. The desats were an indication she needed to go back on the CPAP.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was warm then and well perfused following two low normal temperatures of 36.6. She had tolerated her feeds during the day with a couple of small possets. I mentioned the blood in her stool and [Dr B]'s involvement. The plan was to observe her for the time being, with a low threshold for intervention if required. That just meant that we would inform the doctors at an early stage of any issues. I finished by stating that mum had
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: been there most of the day attending to cares and dad visited that evening. I handed over to Jo Williams that night.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The next date I have been asked about was 5 September 2015."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll go to the corresponding note of that in a moment:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was on a night shift that night and was the designated nurse for part of the night. Again, I have had the chance to review [Baby I]'s notes from that date and my recollections are purely from those notes as I have no personal recollection of that shift. I have checked and I was on with Yvonne Griffiths, [Nurse E], Lucy Letby and Val Thomas. We had two intensive care babies, two high dependency unit babies and three special care babies, so we were quite high acuity for the people who we had on at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "From looking at the notes and shift records, I can't understand the allocation of babies that night and so I wonder if I was in charge of that shift. The shift records I have access to are only in black and white. If they were in colour and I was shown in blue then that would mean I was in charge, but I can't tell from the records I have. I have seen a colour copy of the roster provided by a police officer, which confirms that I was allocated to be shift leader that shift."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, if we could please put from the additional notes page J13858. We see [Nurse C]'s initials and reading her statement, she states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I took [Baby I] over from Val Thomas at 20.30 hours because she was obviously deteriorating, but I then handed over again at 00.30 hours to Yvonne Griffiths and I can't remember why I have done that.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I'm wondering if I took her on because at the time there was no one else to have her and then handed her over as soon as I was able to do so, so I could concentrate on being in charge of the unit. The fact that Val had her first would indicate she was quite well at that stage. The notes that I did make stated she was deteriorating..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And we can see that on the screen, members of the jury:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "... and likely to need ventilator support. I described her as very quiet and desaturating frequently, especially at handover on handling. Her capillary refill time was 2 seconds, which is okay. She was pale and she was slightly mottled. Her abdomen was full, fairly firm to touch at that time, and she was desaturating when palpated.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bowel sounds were heard and I noted she had opened her bowels and been passing urine well on the day shift. She was given oxygen and a paediatric registrar, Dr Ventress, was called to review her."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could pause there and go to Dr Ventress' notes of that review again in the additional file. J13775, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ventress made this note, it would seem, at 22.30 hours, where she sets out the fact that septic screen bloods were taken and antibiotics given. She sets out the blood test results and then records:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Twenty minutes after feed (22.20) had profound desat down to 50% sats. Oxygen provide to 100% and Optiflow at a rate of up to 7 litres a minute and improved to 80%. Stomach was aspirated after which her sats normalised and oxygen weaned down rapidly back to 30%."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Go to the next page, Mr Murphy, where the note continues:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On examination the baby was quiet. She cried when disturbed but not an [unusual] strong cry. The baby looks pale, slightly mottled, and her capillary refill time was less than 2 seconds. There was minimal increased work of breathing. Good bilateral air entry. Chest clear. Heart..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I've forgotten what HS stands for.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Heart sounds.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I thought that. I leave it to others to attach meaning to the numbers:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Abdomen mildly distended but soft. Veiny in appearance. Normal tone."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The impression was that she was a septic baby, so the plan was to give her a fluid bolus, keep her on Optiflow, to repeat the gas in 2 hours' time, or sooner if there were concerns, a lumbar puncture test was required, and a question as to whether she would be given a blood transfusion in the morning, and there would be a need for both chest and abdominal X-rays.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go down again, Dr Ventress saw [Baby I] and she made a note, a further note written retrospectively at 01.00 hours with Dr Ventress recording:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At approximately 23.15 [Baby I] had another profound desat to 50%. Facial oxygen 100% applied with pressure via mask at which her heart rate increased but her sats remained low, so
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: ventilation was given with double-handed jaw thrust, which improved saturation levels gradually.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Decision made to intubate [Baby I]. While equipment was being gathered, [Baby I] improved so the oxygen provided was reduced to 60% with regular resps [I think that says] on the mask with CPAP. She was given high levels of oxygen and have decided to electively intubate with intubation drugs. First attempt was unsuccessful but second attempt, using a size 3 tube, passed easily and there was thereafter good bilateral air entry with the tube at 8 centimetres. Her heart rate and saturation levels improved. Capnograph test was positive. The tube was secured and ventilation settings were determined and then reduced because it would seem the baby was fighting vent and settled better on this."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ventress revised the plan:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Chest X-ray, second morphine bolus, followed by an infusion. Further (inaudible: coughing) tests (inaudible: coughing) 30 minutes. Postpone planned lumbar puncture for now until the baby is more stable. The baby should remain nil by mouth and receive fluids intravenously."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And [Dr B] was asked to come and review the baby and due to acute desaturation -- and Dr Ventress planned to update the parents.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So pausing there, I go back to [Nurse C]'s statement where she said that Dr Ventress was called to review:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She assessed her [that is to say [Baby I]] and was happy with her abdomen and described it as soft when examined. She was happy for [Baby I] to continue to feed at that time. Intravenous cefotaxime was started as per policy in case she had an infection. [Baby I]'s temperature had been cool earlier and had only warmed up slightly. She had been handled for a peripheral intravenous catheter insertion and screen. She had her incubator temperature increased and blankets were added. Losing temperature can be a sign of infection, especially in a baby who desaturates like she was doing, especially on handling.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Therefore sepsis was a concern. I noted that mum and dad were present at the time of her deterioration and were up to date with her cares and plans. [Baby I] had further episodes of desaturation to between 50 and 70%, needing oxygen and positive end expiratory pressure, which is pressure given with a mask which helps to keep the airways open, making it easy for the baby to breathe. Optiflow was increased to 7 litres a minute and she required an inspired oxygen fraction up to 100% for short periods. Her desaturations were worse following feeds. It is
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: something to note because having filled their tummies up, are we squishing their lungs, which can make it harder to breathe or there could be something wrong with the bowel and more problems could be caused by putting feeds in. There are lots of different reasons for desats after feeds but it is worth noting."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The notes state that:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A nasogastric tube was aspirated with minimal results and she had a further desaturation to 55% at 23.15 hours and found it difficult to recover so the decision was taken to intubate her and that decision was taken by the registrar. She was also given a fluid bolus of 0.9% saline for perfusion. We give that for signs of circulatory compromise but I can't say what that is from looking at the notes but maybe poor perfusion or high heart rate. It can be low blood pressure but the notes state her blood pressure had remained stable throughout.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was intubated with a [3-millimetre] tube and put on an end tidal carbon dioxide monitor device to indicate whether carbon dioxide is present in the ET tube. This shows that the tube is in the lungs. She had equal air entry on both sides but was quieter on the left side, so the airway tube was pulled back and better air entry was heard. It was pulled back slightly more following a chest X-ray.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We pulled it back initially because if you put it down too far, it is likely to go into the right lung rather than the left. Because of the way the trachea splits down into each lung it makes it easier to go into the right first. Measurement-wise, there are all sorts of formulas for older children and adults for how far you put the tube down, but if a baby is under 1 you are talking very small distances.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Pulling a tube back or pushing it down only a centimetre makes a massive difference in a baby that size, so when intubating, the registrar will make an estimate. They can see when a tube goes through the vocal cords and know when it is down into the lungs, but whilst they do that they have the baby's head extended back so when released the head will move down and the tube will move slightly. That's partly why we use the end tidal device to check if it's in the lungs and then the X-ray will tell us where in the lungs it is.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "You can see the tube and where it is sat in relation to markers such as rib level, vertebrae level, and you can sometimes see the end, which tells you it's in the right place. Once you're happy with the position you don't secure it with tape, like in an older child, you use a plastic device that sits on the tube that's tied to a hat, so that means you can undo a little clamp and push or pull the tube as you need to."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Turning to the cares given to [Baby I]:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She had two morphine boluses, one pre-intubation and one post as she was very active, to help calm her down. I then noted that she was settled after that and syncing with the ventilator, which meant she wasn't fighting it.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She remained cool and her capillary refill was 2 to 3 seconds, which had got a bit worse. I noted that her peripheries were pale and mottled and a further fluid bolus was given.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The mottled appearance is a sign of a baby who is compromised. You see it in all sorts of things like a baby who is struggling to breathe where the body is getting the oxygen to the important parts. Babies who are cold can appear mottled and some babies who are septic can also look mottled. It is a sign of circulation problems.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was given metronidazole, which is another antibiotic, so she was then on two different antibiotics, which focus on different things. Cefotaxime is for babies over 72 hours old who are showing signs of sepsis. The metronidazole is for babies with abdominal problems such as NEC, which is something we see quite a lot on the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The notes show that the parents were updated and had to come in to stay on the unit overnight. The reducing substances result was flagged to the senior paediatric registrar who was then going to follow up that with further tests that may have been ordered and who would then advise us regarding any action needed. I have been unable to find the reducing substances result and can only presume it is not on the system.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "They do come through electronically but it can take a while. If there is something we need to be aware of then they will pass the result verbally, for example if a baby has low platelets. I cannot remember how they came through in this instance.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We would tell the result to the registrar whether they were good or bad. A reducing substance test is a stool sample test used to diagnose lactose intolerance and some rare metabolic abnormalities. The notes also reflect that mum had also said that she thought that [Baby I]'s urine output had been less than usual that afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I then handed over care for [Baby I] to Yvonne Griffiths at 00.30 hours. As I said earlier, I can't recall why I handed [Baby I] over to Yvonne.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have also been asked whether I recall a conversation with [Baby I]'s mum on an occasion when she had come back into the unit after [Baby I] had died. She came back to the unit to drop money off that they had raised. I do remember that conversation. It was about the fact that I had looked after [Baby I] the night before she had died and she had been very unsettled and had been throughout the day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was in an incubator and all undressed and babies hate that, generally speaking, so I had dressed her. That must have been after mum had gone home. I hoped it would settle her down because they get cosy and it did work a little bit. When mum came in after [Baby I] died, we spoke and she asked me about why I had dressed her and I explained that I wanted to see if it would settle her. I don't recall any other part of the conversation and I don't remember saying to her that [Baby I] didn't die of prematurity. I only remember the babygro part of the conversation."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And that's the extent of the relevant parts of [Nurse C]'s statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR SALLY OGDEN (read)
Next, my Lord, and overleaf at page 38 of the reading bundle, is a statement from Dr Sally Ogden.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Before we get to the body of her statement -- and if we return, please, Mr Murphy, to the carousel, tile number 5 -- we will see, though it's not within the statement, Dr Sally Ogden made some clinical notes about [Baby I] upon her arrival within Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we click on, please, Mr Murphy. We're going back here to 18 August. Scroll down. We can see it's a note of the reception in Liverpool Women's, the active problems, condition at birth, and then a familiar set of entries: ventilation, cardiovascular, feeding regime, screening, cultures, ultrasound, jaundice resolved, blood results, long line in situ, medication, Dr Ogden's examination of [Baby I]:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Pink and well perfused, abdomen soft and not distended."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Then the plan for [Baby I] at that point in time was to continue on CPAP and wean her off as able, to increase her feeds and to repeat the cranial ultrasound.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was Dr Ogden's examination of [Baby I] upon her return. Then her statement, dated 22 May 2019, moves forward in time to 23 August 2015. If Mr Murphy could please put up the
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: corresponding clinical notes, which are in the additional file and can be found at page J13760 and 13761.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Sally Ogden's note begins at the bottom. Now I will read from the statement if I may:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My notes begin with me stating I had been asked to review her abdomen. That happened fairly frequently on the neonatal unit. At any time there was any concern about abdominal distension, we would always have to look at the baby to see if there were any signs of infection, so that will have been why I reviewed [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I stated that there had been some concerns about her abdomen being distended. The nasogastric tube had been repositioned after an X-ray and now the abdomen felt softer and no longer distended. They had got some air and some mucus out of the tummy and now it was soft with palpable bowel loops, which are quite common in preterms babies, where you can feel the loops of the bowel within the abdomen because the abdominal walls are quite thin, but it wasn't tense or distended and there was no discomfort on palpation."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If you go down the page, Mr Murphy, if you don't mind. Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I documented that an X-ray had been done, which I reviewed. The nasogastric tube was in too far into the stomach, which is why I had repositioned. The bowel loops looked normal and I signed that at 23.00 hours."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: As we can see. Down the page, please:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My next entry..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That doesn't appear to be Dr Ogden's note. It's at 23.00 hours, her statement tells us. It says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My next entry read: 'Nasogastric tube repositioned since Xray.' I don't remember who raised the concern about [Baby I]'s abdomen but it most likely would have been one of the nurses who were looking after her. Looking back, it looked like the senior house officer had reviewed her first, and that was Emily Thomas, so it could have been her who raised it to me."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look back at the top of page 13760, we'll see an entry from Dr Emily Thomas. Thank you. I'll return to Dr Ogden's statement while we have that on screen:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "So it looked like Emily was asked to review her earlier by nursing staff as she had a distended abdomen and some blood in
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: her stool earlier that day. She had no aspirates coming out of the NG tube, was full and quite tense, and Emily had requested the X-ray, which I subsequently reviewed.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It is quite common for the nursing staff to raise concerns with one of us and if it was an SHO who had seen the baby then, as a registrar, you would go and see the baby afterwards. It seems with [Baby I] that since we had re-passed the NG tube her abdomen was a lot softer and there were no concerning features on examination of the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "NG tubes can be positioned wrongly but they don't tend to cause loads of difficulty, but sometimes if they are not in the right place it just means you can't get air out of the tummy. The point of the NG tube as well as for feeding is also to get air from the stomach, so if it's not sitting in the right place and then you're not getting air out, that could contribute to her abdomen being distended.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Because the nursing staff put them in reasonably blindly through the nose to an estimated length, it is not unusual for it to be a bit far or a bit short. Having passed a tube, you then take an aspirate from it and if it's acidic then it proves that it is in the stomach. But because a lot of these babies have X-rays for other reasons, you always see where it is on the X-ray. They probably get X-rays once a week where you could see the position of the tube, but you wouldn't normally routinely Xray every NG tube.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "An NG tube can deflate the stomach, especially on CPAP, but only if it is not clamped. I can't say if it was or wasn't in this case. It can drain on free drainage and will do increasingly when aspirated. There are many times that the NG tube can be clamped, unclamped, on free drainage, aspirated. It is all part of the continuing assessment of what is needed at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In [Baby I]'s case it wasn't that the tube was in the wrong place, it was just that it wasn't deflating the air properly, so it will have been in the stomach. It was just potentially in too far and was curling on itself or not in far enough.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her abdomen did get better once the NG was re-passed, but it might have got better anyway if it was just a transient problem due to CPAP. It is difficult to say retrospectively when there is only what is documented in the notes, but the more important aspect at the time was the abdomen was then soft, so unlikely to be a significant cause rather than the specifics of the NG tube.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When Emily wrote there were no aspirates, I think she clearly meant there were no abnormal aspirates. We get worried about NEC
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: and babies who get a lot of bile back up the tube or green aspirates or blood up the tube or large quantities of aspirates. For example, if you're feeding a baby 2ml of food but are aspirating 10ml, then it is clear it is not going anywhere. But Emily doesn't say any of that so I presume her record was a reassuring sign that whatever the nurses were feeding into the stomach was being digested rather than just sitting there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "If you get no aspirates, you wouldn't use that as a sign that the NG tube is in the wrong place, so you would tend to X-ray.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It appeared that the small procedure of repositioning [Baby I]'s NG tube resolved the issue of her distended abdomen. What we tend to find with babies with NEC is that their abdomens stay distended, so even if we hadn't repositioned the NG tube, the fact that her tummy got better in such a short space of time was reassuring that there wasn't more significant pathology going on. I would have been more concerned if the X-ray had shown abnormal bowel loops rather than specifically anything to do with the NG tube.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "That was the last of my involvement with [Baby I] that night. In summary, the NG tube being repositioned and the distended stomach was something that happened quite frequently and not something I was overly concerned about. There was nothing about this episode that struck me as anything other than routine neonatal management."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly.

Witness statement of MS YVONNE GRIFFITHS (read)
I'm going to begin by reading a statement from Yvonne Griffiths, please, which appears at the front of that most recent bundle.

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Her statement is dated 2 December 2019 and reads as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked by DC Birch of Cheshire Police about my recollection and knowledge of [Baby I]'s care on 5 September 2015. Prior to providing this statement I have had the opportunity to review [Baby I]'s notes for that date.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After reading the notes, I do remember the evening but not the full ins and outs. I remember her parents coming in and providing comfortable armchairs for them to spend time at the bedside.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was on a night shift on 5 September and took over the care of [Baby I] from 00.30 hours on 6 September from [Nurse C]. I then handed her over to the day staff the following morning.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As a senior nurse we tend to take ITU babies or high dependency babies when they are allocated, so on that evening I had a high dependency baby on Optiflow when I first came in in nursery 1. [Nurse C] was in charge and was in charge of coordinating the night and any admissions that come through, or if a baby deteriorated then she was responsible for reallocating staff according to need.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The other staff on duty were [Nurse E], Lucy Letby and Val Thomas, who was a nursery nurse. Val would have been responsible for any transition care babies that night if we had any, but I'm not sure if we did. The amount of staff on duty was quite a good ratio to the number of babies we had.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Looking at [Baby I]'s notes for the day I can see [Nurse C] took over at 20.00 hours. I remember coming on duty and [Baby I] had been desaturating during the day a little bit, which is what premature babies do. After all, she was only 28 days old.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was deemed unsuitable for a nursery nurse to take over her care for the night. I think she then became more apnoeic and desaturated quite a bit so she did then need ITU care. As [Nurse C] was the shift leader, she then allocated [Baby I] to be under my care as I had a high dependency baby so was in a position to take over. We work within a team and I'm sure I supported [Nurse C] whilst [Baby I] was intubated before I took over. I remember that we contacted her parents at home. We knew the parents really well and they asked if they could come in because they were very proactive parents. That wasn't a problem at all and I remember them coming in and [Dr B] coming in.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Alison Ventress was the registrar on duty and she's very experienced as well. Everything went to plan with the intubation, however during the night there were episodes of further desaturation which required us to increase the ventilator pressures slightly.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My notes from the night were written retrospectively at 06.19 hours on the 6th. They confirm I took over care at 00.30 hours. She, [Baby I], had been in one of the outer nurseries but when she came to me, she came into nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was on ventilator support and SIMV [that's the reference to mechanical ventilation] 16/5 and 40 breaths per minute. This is simultaneous support which allows the baby to do some of the breathing whilst having mechanical support, so it doesn't take over completely. Because she was a small baby we didn't want to use a lot of high pressures initially because it can cause problems like pneumothoraces because they have only tiny lungs. We start with a lower pressure and then assess with blood gases to see if we need to go up.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A chest X-ray was then performed and the ET tube was pulled back by half a centimetre. My next note was about a desaturation episode at 03.23 hours when her blood gases dropped to 30% oxygen, which we picked up on the monitor that measures oxygen levels. Dr Ventress was already at the bedside and we did inflation breaths using Neopuff. When a baby desats you do a whole check, making sure the probe is on in the first place, then listening to the chest sounds to see if the tube was still in situ, because they wriggle about and sometimes the tube can be dislodged, so we always do those basics and then if everything is checked out okay, we may think they might need a higher pressure. We will disconnect from the ventilator and then pop the bagging mask on and give higher inflation breaths at our control rather than by the ventilator. That can be done by a doctor or a QIS nurse, who's a nurse who's gone through her advanced training like me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regard to that particular desaturation where we bagged [Baby I], I can't recall who was there present and who assisted or who did what.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Following on from that desat, after the Neopuff good air entry was heard and increased pressure required. She had recovered sufficiently to be put back on the ventilator. Ventilation was increased to 20/5. The 20 is the higher pressure, the lower figure is the CPAP. The CPAP just keeps your lungs just open a little bit to make breathing easier and the higher pressure is how much you want to inflate the lungs.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was on 60 breaths per minute, which is normal. She remained very pale and had a similar episode at 0.10 hours. The paleness could have been indicative of NEC, an infection, as she had been started on metronidazole. She also had a blood transfusion overnight via a peripheral cannula and was given 20ml of blood per kilogram of body weight. That was in relation to her
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: paleness and we would have done bloods and possibly her haemoglobin was low.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The note then states that fluids were infusing via another cannula at 150ml per kilogram. These were her maintenance fluids, including morphine. In order to infuse blood products a separate cannula is required. My notes go on to say that preductal oxygen was recorded due to her desaturations. This is to do with the valves in the heart and we have to check pre- and post-ductal stats. We are always looking to see what the cause of the desaturation is.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her temperature was noted to be low, which could have been environmental due to procedures being carried out or early signs of sepsis. Her desaturations, her coolness and the paleness all pointed towards infection and NEC on that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When she was later transferred to Liverpool, we were informed her endotracheal tube was blocked, which was very unusual to happen in an eight-hour window.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My last note was about mum ringing the unit and asking if they could stay over. We encouraged them to come in and they came in. We offered them the parent accommodation but they wanted to be with her, so we set them up with chairs next to her bed.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Dr B] updated them as to what had happened and I noted they were very loving and appropriate at the bedside. I can't think of anything else that may assist the investigation."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, we can return to the original bundle, please, page 41.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS NICOLA SIMMONS (read)
It's a statement from Nicola Simmons, dated 16 March 2020. She says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked to make comment about a particular baby that I cared for, namely [Baby I], at the Liverpool Women's Hospital in 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In 2015, as band 5 nurse, I was working at Liverpool Women's Hospital neonatal unit when at some time during the late afternoon of 6 September 2015, according to medical notes, I did receive or admit [Baby I] from the transport team to the neonatal unit at the Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We received [Baby I] from the level 2 Countess of Chester Hospital as they would not have been able to ventilate her. We
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: are a level 3 unit and we have a higher level of intensive care support.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My role in 2015 as a neonatal nurse would have been to work with the medical team, admitting babies and setting up ventilation, medication, supporting parents and general nursing of babies. I cannot remember who I was working with on this day. I make this statement purely based on [Baby I]'s medical notes that I have reviewed and were typed by me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My medical notes relating to [Baby I] timed at 18.50 on 6 September 2015 show that I admitted her from the transport team. They show that [Baby I] was, on arrival, 31 weeks, incubated, ventilated and in receipt of two peripheral cannulas. She was also nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was then transferred to a Liverpool Women's Hospital incubator and a ventilator was set up for [Baby I]. As the receiving nurse, I and the medical staff would have been given a handover of [Baby I]'s condition from the transport team.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The notes say not long after the transfer from the transport team and at the Liverpool Women's Hospital, with [Baby I] having been set up on our own ventilator and whilst we were setting up a new intravenous line for [Baby I] to receive total parenteral nutrition, [Baby I] had a profound bradycardia upon positioning.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "This in itself is not uncommon for a small sick baby upon repositioning. For a tiny baby like [Baby I] just moving her from one incubator to another, as we had to, may have triggered a desaturation and a bradycardia. The movement upset could have been created by as little as moving her arm so we can get access for a line insertion.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From the notes, [Baby I] had large creamy secretions in her ET tube, possibly as a direct result of being moved. These secretions can block the airway. I would have listened to [Baby I]'s breathing to discover that she had secretions blocking her airway. These desaturations and bradycardias can be a natural reaction to being moved. However, they do indicate to me and the medical team that there is something very wrong with that baby.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "This reaction is how the babies tell us that something is not right. The fact that [Baby I] had a bradycardia along with a desaturation tells me that there was an issue with her airway and she was not able to breathe, she is not able to circulate herself. I would have reacted by giving [Baby I] suction in order for her to breathe.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The notes say that [Baby I] was a little irritable and had abdomen problems. The abdomen problem could have caused [Baby I]
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: pain and discomfort. I cannot recall this bradycardia episode at all let alone who I was working with.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Interpreting [Baby I]'s notes, [Baby I] recovered from this episode. According to the notes I changed [Baby I]'s morphine. It's standard practice that if a baby arrives with certain infusions running, like morphine or adrenaline drugs, we will replace those drugs with our own Women's Hospital comparable drugs via a doctor's prescription.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I]'s antibiotics were also changed. [Baby I] was also on 10% dextrose, again which was changed to Liverpool Women's Hospital. Later on in the day, [Baby I] had settled and we have supported her parents."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 10 September 2018, DC Birch from Cheshire Police interviewed me and asked me about the night of 30 September and my recollections and involvement with [Baby I] on that date. I was informed that [Baby I] suffered a collapse at handover time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Of course, I remember [Baby I] well in general terms because she was on the unit for quite some time and had a number of collapses. I knew her because, as a team leader, you need to have an overview of all the babies but I don't remember being heavily involved in her care.

blocks.text: "I have been told that I am shown on the rota for 30 September as being on nights. blocks.text: "I can't recall what the handover procedure was at the time, whether it was a five-minute huddle by the nurse station or whether we all went to the resource room. blocks.text: My Lord, a statement dated 3 April 2019, and [Dr A] says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked by DC Birch from Cheshire Police about my recollections of and involvement with a baby called [Baby I], who died on 23 October 2015 at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked in particular about 30 September 2015. Prior to providing this statement I have had the opportunity to review [Baby I]'s clinical notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As far as any recollection of [Baby I], I can say that I remember that she was there at the start of my placement in Chester and I remember the name, but that's about it. Anything that appears in the following statement is exclusively from my notes and not from personal recollection.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My notes on 30 September 2015 start at 16.30 hours. It actually looks like I've started to write 17.00 but I've crossed that out and wrote 16.30."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I wonder if we can go, please, to tile 97, Mr Murphy, and the notes behind.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see in the top left-hand corner that amendment that the doctor has just mentioned in his statement. And from his notes the statement continues as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My note on that date states that I was asked to see [Baby I] due to her vomiting and desaturating. I was crash called to the neonatal intensive care unit following a large vomit. I don't know who crash called me because it comes through the switchboard and they just tell you where to go.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was being bagged on a resuscitator and oral and nasal suction was given. Her saturations were 30% and her heart rate 50. On my arrival, I recorded that she was in a heated cot and had been weaned in the last 24 hours. The baby had been cool that day and her temperature had been monitored on a heated cot at 38 degrees with the incubator set at 20 degrees.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The fact that I have managed to write it in that order would suggest that I have dealt with the problem first and was doing my writing afterwards. I have set the scene at the top and then, on my arrival, given my impression of what was going on at that point. I probably started to write at 17.00 but this is an event from 16.30 so I have changed it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The large vomit had already happened and her oxygen saturations have reduced down as far as 30% and that is really low. Her heart rate has followed that as well. With a low saturation, a low heart rate follows. When I arrived she was pink and her heart rate was 130. Saturations were 99% in air, so she didn't need any extra oxygen, and she had normal saturations with a normal heart rate. Her respiratory rate was 28 and she would have been about 34 weeks, so a respiratory rate of 28 was normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When I was looking at her, she was breathing well, there was no effort for breathing and she wasn't working hard. Her chest signs was clear, her abdomen was a little bit distended, and she had active bowel signs all over.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The fontanelle, the soft spot at the top, was normal. Her tone was normal, her movements were normal. A cannula was placed in the back of her left hand."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can scroll down a little bit, please, Mr Murphy. There will be a plan at the bottom of the notes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My notes then reflect what my plan was for her. I have ordered some blood tests, a full blood count and a CRP as markers of infection, and a blood culture for presumed infection. I arranged a chest and an abdominal X-ray to look for why she had a vomit and a big desaturation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have also said, and this is in quotation marks, 'Let's not feed her and let's give her all of her fluids as IV fluids through that cannula.' She was on 165ml per kilogram per day, which I presume would be what she was on by(?) milk prior to this. So it's the same volume, it's just a different fluid via a different route.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Then we've started some intravenous antibiotics. There are some ticks next to them on my notes and that means I have ordered them. My notes then say 'venous gas' and she had a lactate of 5.4, which was raised. She had a base excess of minus 6.7, which is also raised, and this has come at the time she had her collapse, so they are not surprising results, but they are very difficult to quantify given that she had recently been unwell. Lactate is a marker of how your cells are doing their metabolism. Without oxygen, you switch to an anaerobic metabolism and it's a marker of that. It's often raised in sepsis and it's often raised if you've had an event recently. The base excess would normally be between plus 2 and minus 2. The lactate I wouldn't normally expect to be over 2, so 5.4 is quite high, but again there was a reason for it in that she had just needed some resuscitation. Whether that preceded the collapse or whether it's because of the collapse, it's impossible to tell on that gas."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down a little further, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Dr A] says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My next entry was at 20.00 hours on the same date, the 30th. The chest X-ray showed perihilar shadowing. That's where all of the airways or the blood vessels that join the lungs into the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: main breathing apparatus and to the main blood vessels have some increased markings.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "This could be consistent with infection and the fact that I have mentioned it means that it wasn't normal, but without seeing the X-ray I can't comment any more. There was no evidence, or I have not written of any evidence, of any collapse or signs of bits of lung that were obscured by infection.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I then wrote with regards to the abdominal film that there were dilated loops of bowel in the lower quadrant but there was no air in the biliary tree and no obvious falciform ligament."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: What does all that mean? Can someone else help us later in relation to that if it's of significance?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think we've encountered falciform ligament before.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, or biliary tree. We'll ask one of the doctors to help us, thank you:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "So that was looking at the air in the loops of bowel because it's gone in the top end and it'll work its way out at the bottom end. This showed there was no air in the biliary tree. The gall bladder is connected to your bowel over in the upper right-hand quadrant. If you've got free air, you'll often see that tracking back up and that will be a worrying sign of NEC, necrotising enterocolitis, but I couldn't see that there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She did have temperature instability and she'd had an apnoea where she stopped breathing, so my presumption was that this was the very early stages of NEC, so that was why I ordered the tests that were ordered and why I started her on antibiotics. My notes show a triangle next to where I wrote 'NEC', which is medical shorthand for showing that is my diagnosis."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see that in the bottom of the left page:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I then wrote, 'Presumed NEC Bell score of 1A.' There is a scoring system for necrotising enterocolitis and, based on the X-ray and the other things that are there, I have looked it up and I have typed it as a 1A, which is a very, very low score.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "If it had been NEC that had been ongoing for a while, you'd have a score that was higher, so 2 or 3. So in terms of the 1A, that's only suspected NEC. She wasn't displaying any signs of NEC, but there was enough there to make me want to treat it to prevent it getting any worse. Even if there is a very, very low
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: suspicion of NEC, you still take the safe option and treat it as if it was. I wouldn't want to have missed it and then found ourselves with a higher score and a baby that was worsening. So the cefotaxime, which was the antibiotic started at the end of that review earlier on, was now supplemented by metronidazole, which is another antibiotic. They both cover different spheres of bugs, so it was a two-pronged approach.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There is a sticker on the notes..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can go to tile 98, please:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... which relates to the X-ray review. My comments on that are the same as in my notes, but the sticker is a sure mark that I have seen it. After that sticker, my last note was that mother had been updated. I then signed off the notes."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Take that down, thank you:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am trying to picture the baby or parents [continues [Dr A]] and I can't recall the appearance of any of them, so the fact that I've written 'mother updated' at the bottom of my notes, that may well have been my only discussion with that family. At that point I will have finished for the daytime and handed over to Dave Harkness, who was on for the night, and he makes the next entries on [Baby I]'s notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have also looked through [Baby I]'s other notes and know that she was there for quite a while, as you would expect for a 27week gestation baby. I remember her name because even though I didn't look after her day-to-day, I would have heard her name at handover when she got mentioned, but there's still nothing that stands out about her to me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "An explanation for her large vomit on 30 September could be because her bowel could have been inflamed, possibly a sign of early necrotising enterocolitis. The Bell score of 1A would have been increased by having blood in the vomit or bile in the vomit or blood passing from the tail end. She had a large vomit and a desaturation and in a baby who has had temperature instability that day, that could be a sign of NEC. So based on the vomit, temperature instability, presumed apnoea because of the desaturation and the low heart rate, they were all my warning flags that this could be NEC, so you start the investigations and start treatment.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Having looked through the rest of her notes, I am unable to comment on whether there was anything unusual about the desaturation of a baby of that gestation without being there to see it happen because it happened before I arrived. As the doctor, you come along after things have happened and deal with
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: what's in front of you. You come up with a care plan and implement that. There will have been some information passed at the time of arriving there, but if a baby has sats in the 30s with a heart rate in the 50s, it is more important to get on with treating the baby there and then, and then afterwards tell me what happened before.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I will presume that there was some extra information given at that point about the temperature instability and about the large vomit, which has then made me put my pieces together to think this could be necrotising enterocolitis. I can't remember who would have given me that additional information.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As far as discussing [Baby I] with other members of staff, there will obviously been a discussion with Dave Harkness for the night shift because we've started some investigations. She will have been on the list of babies to keep a closer eye on that night. I can't think of anything else that might assist with the investigation at this time."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: But my Lord, for the sake of completeness, please, if we can go to tile 204, there is in fact another entry from [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm going to rely on the analyst's summary given his handwriting and the note reads:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Previous care noted. 9 o'clock the next morning."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Presumably the doctor on the day shift the following day again:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Previous care noted. See medical notes for full details. Imp 1. Presumed NEC. Plan..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, that should be "impression 1, presumed NEC":
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Plan. (1) Nil by mouth. (2) CRP at 18.00 hours. (3) 3 days of antibiotics. Review to consider restarting feeds. Parents concerned that sibling has lactose intolerance [query] related to episode of abdo distension."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Observations: alert, active, pink, well perfused, heart rate 150. Saturation of oxygen 97% (air). Femorals ++. Respiratory rate 30 to 40. Equal air entry bilaterally."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Resp distress. Vesicular sounds all zones. Abdomen soft, markedly less distended. Active bowel sounds all quadrants. LKKS..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which I'm told is liver, kidney, kidney, spleen -- I will be corrected, I'm sure, if I'm wrong -- and a circle indicating they were palpable:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Reducible umbilical hernia. Anterior fontanelle. Sort(?) tone N..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which is "no" presumably -- sorry "normal". Then the next word is not legible:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... movements normal."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that concludes [Dr A]'s contribution for events on and around 30 September.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, the next witness is Bernadette Butterworth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: BUTTERWORTH

blocks.text: That's the oxygen level in the blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Her oxygen level and she came bradycardic, so her heart rate dropped.

blocks.text: Right.

blocks.text: I don't think she was breathing at that point. At some point her chest -- there was no chest movement so we started intervening with the Neopuff.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because the alarm monitor would have alarmed, the monitor would have alarmed and we would have --

blocks.text: And do you remember what you were both doing or what you were doing at the time the alarms went off?

blocks.text: We probably would have been just handing over.

blocks.text: So literally in the process of discussing what had gone on and what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BUTTERWORTH

blocks.text: -- you needed to be aware of? Okay, all right. So the alarm's alerted you to a number of problems with [Baby I]?

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Um... We'd got the Neopuff, I had started Neopuffing -- I think it was me who started Neopuffing. I noticed [Baby I]'s tummy was becoming larger, chest wasn't moving, so I asked Lucy to aspirate the NG tube.

blocks.text: Let's pause there. So when you went for the Neopuff, just to be clear, was [Baby I] on any respiratory support at all at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BUTTERWORTH

blocks.text: So she wasn't receiving any --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BUTTERWORTH

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: BUTTERWORTH

blocks.text: My fault, I didn't want to interrupt you, but you've -- I think one or two people might be struggling to hear.

blocks.text: My fault, not yours. Please don't apologise.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 29 September 2015, a weekly review with consultant of the week, Dr Newby, was completed. [Baby I] at this point was doing well. She was given fortified vitamins in her milk, she was gaining weight nicely and taking bottle feeds.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I] had been pale but we were happy with her. There were no concerns in her blood tests. It was planned for the following week for routine immunisations and she was coming up to 2 months old. [Baby I] was in a hospital cot, which maintains body temperature. [Baby I] was doing okay.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 30 September 2015, the consultant made a plan on the information provided. In general, if a child is well and there are no concerns, they will not visit the child personally, which is the norm.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 11.40 hours on 30 September, [Baby I]'s temperature had come down slightly to 36.2. We like to keep babies at 36.5. Other than being pale, which fits with anaemia, her abdomen was slightly larger than typical for a baby. However, the senior house officer examined her the day before and it was the same, so there was nothing to worry about as she had opened her bowels. The plan was to watch and see how she got on.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 16.30 hours on the 30th, [Baby I] vomited, her oxygen levels dropped, and she stopped breathing. She required some assistance with her breathing by bagging, which in essence is giving breathing via a mask to help breathe for her for a few minutes. [Baby I]'s oxygen levels and heart rate dropped quite a lot, which typically happens when there is a pause in breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Once resolved, the decision was for [Baby I] to have a septic screen, which means putting her on antibiotics, followed by an X-ray of her chest and abdomen. They stopped her milk as when there are breathing problems we tend to give babies a rest and give them fluids instead. [Baby I]'s blood gas was quite high, which goes along with an infection or necrotising enterocolitis, NEC. Her chest X-ray showed her abdomen was quite large and her bowel loops were prominent. Initially, this indicates NEC, so they started [Baby I] with an extra antibiotic which helps to fight the bugs that can cause NEC. [Baby I] was still breathing for herself.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I saw [Baby I] at 22.00 hours on 30 September. I went to see her for a routine review because of the events in the day. She was breathing well for herself, the blood tests did not show any indication of obvious signs of infection. She was still receiving antibiotics and she still looked pale. [Baby I] did not like being touched or being handled to change her nappy, which again suggested an infection.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her abdomen was still distended and you could see visible loops, which means they are full of air. The wall of a baby's abdomen is quite thin and you can make out the impression of the bowel underneath. This would look rather lumpy and looks like ridges from the tubes underneath the skin. It is wavy in appearance. I could hear her bowels, which was a good sign, as with severe NEC this can stop your bowels from moving. A repeat of the blood gas lactate had gone down to 1.1, which is good, and there was nothing concerning. The plan was to carry on with what we were doing and try not to handle her too much and to think about giving her a blood transfusion when she was better. A blood transfusion can cause problems with NEC as it can make the blood quite thick, so we tend to hold off until patients are well.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The next day, [Baby I] was seen by [Dr A] again. She was stable, nil by mouth, and further blood tests were requested for later that day and [Baby I] was to continue with antibiotics."

Not everyone will do this on a shift, but as I was on a night shift I tend to if a patient has been unwell during the day or there are any concerns.
